section.title: The Prophet's Grief and Hope
section.sectionRationale: This is the center and turning point of the whole book, the longest and most intricate acrostic, three verses to each Hebrew letter. From the depths of personal anguish under the rod of God, the sufferer reaches the great confession at the heart of Scripture: the loving devotion of the LORD never ceases, His mercies are new every morning. Around that summit the poem gathers grief, hope, repentance, and a cry for vindication.
section.thesis: In the darkest personal suffering under God's hand, the sufferer deliberately calls to mind the steadfast love and unfailing mercies of the LORD, and on that ground he counsels patient waiting, calls the people to repentance, and entrusts his cause to the God who draws near and says, Do not be afraid.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the man under the rod of wrath, 3:1 to 18; the great turn, yet I have hope, His mercies are new every morning, 3:19 to 24; reflections on the goodness and justice of God, 3:25 to 39; a call to examine our ways and return to the LORD, with renewed lament, 3:40 to 54; and the LORD who drew near, with a plea for vindication against the enemies, 3:55 to 66.

units.label: The man under the rod of wrath
units.note: I am the man who has seen affliction

verses.text: I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of God's wrath.
He has driven me away and made me walk in darkness instead of light.
Indeed, He keeps turning His hand against me all day long.
He has worn away my flesh and skin; He has shattered my bones.
He has besieged me and surrounded me with bitterness and hardship.
He has made me dwell in darkness like those dead for ages.
He has walled me in so I cannot escape; He has weighed me down with chains.
Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer.
He has barred my ways with cut stones; He has made my paths crooked.
He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush.
He forced me off my path and tore me to pieces; He left me without help.
He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow.
He pierced my kidneys with His arrows.
I am a laughingstock to all my people; they mock me in song all day long.
He has filled me with bitterness; He has intoxicated me with wormwood.
He has ground my teeth with gravel and trampled me in the dust.
My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is.
So I say, “My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD.”

units.label: Yet I have hope
units.note: His mercies are new every morning

verses.text: Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall.
Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me.
Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope:
Because of the {{chesed|loving devotion}} of the LORD we are not consumed, for His {{rachamim|mercies}} never fail.
They are new every morning; great is Your {{emunah|faithfulness}}!
“The LORD is my {{cheleq|portion}},” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in Him.”

units.label: The LORD is good
units.note: on waiting, and the justice of God

verses.text: The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.
It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.
It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young.
Let him sit alone in silence, for the LORD has laid it upon him.
Let him bury his face in the dust, perhaps there is still hope.
Let him offer his cheek to the one who would strike him; let him be filled with reproach.
For the Lord will not cast us off forever.
Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.
For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.
To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the land,
to deny a man justice before the Most High,
to subvert a man in his lawsuit, of these the Lord does not approve.
Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?
Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?
Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?

units.label: Let us return to the LORD

verses.text: Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.
Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven:
“We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.”
You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us; You have killed without pity.
You have covered Yourself with a cloud that no prayer can pass through.
You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.
All our enemies open their mouths against us.
Panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction.
Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people.
My eyes overflow unceasingly, without relief,
until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.
My eyes bring grief to my soul because of all the daughters of my city.
Without cause my enemies hunted me like a bird.
They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.
The waters flowed over my head, and I thought I was going to die.

units.label: You drew near when I called
units.note: the LORD heard, and a plea for justice

verses.text: I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.
You heard my plea: “Do not ignore my cry for relief.”
You drew near when I called on You; You said, “Do not be afraid.”
You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life.
You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me; vindicate my cause!
You have seen all their malice, all their plots against me.
O LORD, You have heard their insults, all their plots against me,
the slander and murmuring of my assailants against me all day long.
When they sit and when they rise, see how they mock me in song.
You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.
Put a veil of anguish over their hearts; may Your curse be upon them!
You will pursue them in anger and exterminate them from under Your heavens, O LORD.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant loyalty. This is one of the richest words in the Old Testament, God's committed, faithful love that will not let His people go. Its range includes love, kindness, mercy, and loyalty to a covenant. It is the ground of all hope in 3:22.

rachamim.gloss: Mercies, tender compassions; the plural of a word related to the womb, evoking the deep, gut level tenderness a mother feels for her child. God's compassions are not worn out by our sin; they never fail and are renewed with each new morning.

emunah.gloss: Faithfulness, firmness, reliability; the word behind our Amen. God's faithfulness is not a mood but a settled, solid dependability. Great is Your faithfulness confesses that God can be leaned on completely, even when everything else has collapsed.

cheleq.gloss: Portion, share, allotted inheritance. In Israel each tribe received a portion of land, but the Levites' portion was the LORD Himself. To say the LORD is my portion is to declare that God, not possessions or circumstances, is one's true and sufficient inheritance.

basic.context: This is the heart of the book, and the most personal chapter. A single sufferer speaks, and he does not spare us: God has become like a bear, a lion, an archer aiming at him; he is walled in, chewed by gravel, drowning in bitterness, and even his prayers seem shut out. He reaches the bottom in verse 18, my hope from the LORD has perished. And then, at the exact center of Lamentations, the whole book turns. He deliberately calls one thing to mind: the LORD's steadfast love never ceases, His mercies are new every morning, great is Your faithfulness. From that summit he counsels patient waiting, calls the people to repent and return, weeps again, and finally rests his case with the God who drew near and said, Do not be afraid.
basic.hermeneutics: The famous words of verses 22 to 23 are not a naive burst of good feeling; they come out of the deepest darkness, and they are a choice. Notice verse 21: yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope. Hope here is an act of remembering God's character on purpose, against the evidence of feelings. The chapter teaches how faith survives suffering: not by denying the pain, which it describes with brutal honesty, but by anchoring to who God is, His covenant love, His endless mercy, His faithfulness, and then waiting, repenting, and praying.
basic.originalLanguages: The turning point rests on a cluster of great Hebrew words. Chesed is the LORD's steadfast, covenant love that never lets go. Rachamim, His mercies, is a word tied to the womb, the deep tenderness a mother feels, and it never runs dry. Emunah is faithfulness, the solid word behind our Amen, God utterly dependable. And cheleq is one's portion or inheritance; to say the LORD is my portion is to make God Himself, not comfort or possessions, one's treasure.
basic.typology: The innocent sufferer who is aimed at like a target, dropped into a pit, has water close over his head, and calls out from the depths anticipates Christ, who was truly innocent, cast into the pit of death, and heard by the Father. God's mercies new every morning point to the new mercy that dawned in the resurrection on the first day of the week. And the LORD is my portion is fulfilled in the believer whose inheritance is Christ Himself.
basic.christ: The sufferer's cry, I called on Your name out of the depths of the Pit, and You drew near and said Do not be afraid, is answered supremely in Jesus. He, the truly innocent one, went down into the pit of death, and the Father heard Him and raised Him. The steadfast love that never ceases is poured out at the cross, where mercy and justice meet, and the new mercies every morning shine brightest in the resurrection dawn. Because the LORD is our portion in Christ, we can never be finally consumed.
basic.god: This chapter gives us one of the fullest portraits of God's heart in the Bible: He is faithful, His love steadfast, His compassions inexhaustible and daily renewed. He is sovereign, both adversity and good come from His mouth, and He is just, He does not approve of injustice and does not willingly afflict. He disciplines, but He will not cast off forever, and He draws near to the crying heart with Do not be afraid.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 42 and 62 model waiting and hoping in God from the depths. Romans 8 says nothing can separate us from God's love. The hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness draws its title from verse 23. Hebrews 12 speaks of the LORD's discipline as a Father's love, and Jonah 2 echoes crying out from the depths.
basic.oneStory: At the very center of the Bible's darkest lament stands its brightest confession of hope: the LORD's love never ceases and His mercies are new every morning. This is the hinge on which the exile, and the whole story of God's dealing with sinners, turns from despair toward hope. It runs forward to Christ, in whom that steadfast love takes flesh, goes down into the pit for us, and rises with mercy new every morning.

context.literary:
The third poem is the book's centre in form as well as in meaning. It has sixty-six verses, three for each letter of the alphabet, so that verses 1 to 3 all begin with aleph, verses 4 to 6 with bet, and so on. The effect is a kind of slowed time: the same letter hammers three times, and the three-fold lines of the earlier poems become three-fold verses.

The form shows what the poet is doing at the turn. Verses 22 to 24 all begin with the letter chet, and they are the verses that name the LORD's covenant love, His new mercies and the sufferer's portion. Verses 25 to 27 all begin with tet, and each starts with the word 'good': 'The LORD is good,' 'It is good to wait quietly,' 'It is good for a man to bear the yoke.' The hope of this chapter is built in the very skeleton of the acrostic.

The speaking voice also moves. In verses 1 to 17 God is called only 'He' and the divine name is not spoken. It first appears in verse 18, 'my hope from the LORD,' at the lowest point, and then again in verses 22, 24 and 25, once the poet has turned. The 'I' of verses 1 to 21 becomes 'we' in verses 22 and 40 to 47, and returns as 'I' in verses 48 to 66, so that the individual's story is offered to the whole community and then taken back.

The chapter is also an arc. Verse 8, 'He shuts out my prayer,' is reversed in verse 56, 'You heard my plea.' The pit of verses 53 to 55 is the end of the walls and darkness of verses 5 to 9, and the poem climbs out of it in a single stanza. Verse 19 asks God to 'remember,' and verse 21 shows the poet remembering God. That is the hinge on which the book turns.
context.historical:
Whoever speaks, the details fit what Jeremiah is known to have suffered. He was put in the stocks, Jeremiah 20:2, and said that he was 'a laughingstock all day long,' Jeremiah 20:7, language close to verse 14, 'a laughingstock to all my people; they mock me in song all day long.' He was lowered into a cistern with no water, only mud, Jeremiah 38:6, and was rescued by the hands of an Ethiopian official, Jeremiah 38:7-13. The pit and stones of verses 53 to 55 recall that scene, though they are also the stock imagery of the psalms of suffering, such as Psalm 88:6. The poem does not name its speaker.

The bitter foods of verse 15, wormwood and poison, are the foods of the covenant curse. Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15 had announced that the LORD would feed the people wormwood and give them poisoned water, and Deuteronomy 29:18 had warned of a root that bears poisonous and bitter fruit. The man who eats them is eating what the nation was told to expect.

Verses 40 to 47 voice the situation of those left in the broken land and the exiles in Babylon, who have begun to ask why. They have not yet seen the return that Jeremiah 29:10 promised after seventy years, and the 'cloud' of verse 44 is a picture of a heaven that prayer cannot reach. The comfort of verse 31, 'the Lord will not cast us off forever,' therefore had to be believed against appearances, without the evidence that the exile would end. The recipients of the poem were learning to live in the time between the sentence and the return.
context.canonical:
Verses 22 and 23 are drawn from the self-description of God at Sinai. In Exodus 34:6-7 the LORD proclaims that He is 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' This was the confession that Moses and Israel relied on after the golden calf, and Nehemiah 9:31 uses it after the exile: 'in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them.' The poet in the middle of ruin reaches for the creed that carried Israel through the first great breach, and finds that it still holds.

The theme of waiting for the LORD runs through the Psalms and the prophets. Psalm 130:5-7 says, 'I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait,' and Micah 7:7-9 says, 'Because I have sinned against Him, I must endure the rage of the LORD, until He argues my case.' Isaiah 54:7-8 gives the answer of the LORD: 'For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back.' Job 13:15 and Habakkuk 3:17-18 are similar acts of choice made in the dark.

The call in verse 40 to examine our ways and turn back is completed in the last chapter, Lamentations 5:21, 'Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return.' The idea that discipline is a father's love is taken up in Hebrews 12:5-6, which quotes Proverbs 3:11-12. The promise that nothing can separate the believer from the love of God, Romans 8:38-39, is the New Testament's reading of verse 22, and James 5:11 calls the Lord 'full of compassion and mercy,' in language that recalls the chapter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants to teach a defeated people how to hope without lying. He does not begin with the hope. He begins with seventeen verses of pain, as though no one could be called to trust God who has not first been allowed to say what God's hand has felt like. Only then does he say, 'Yet I call this to mind,' verse 21. The turn is presented as something done, a deliberate act of recall, and he asks his hearers to do the same.

He also wants to shape the posture of waiting. Verses 25 to 30 are a short course in how to suffer under discipline: wait quietly, bear the yoke, sit alone in silence, bury the face in the dust, 'perhaps there is still hope.' The 'perhaps' matters, since he does not promise a quick end. And in verses 40 to 42 he calls the whole people to examine and turn, so that the personal confession of verses 21 to 24 becomes a public one.

He has one more aim, which is to give a place for the cry for justice. The enemy is not forgotten, verses 59 to 66, and the poem hands the matter to the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first part of the chapter describes what suffering feels like, and it does not describe God as He is. The picture of a bear in ambush, a lion, an archer, a jailer is the sufferer's perception in the dark, and the poem itself corrects it in verses 31 to 33, 'He does not willingly afflict.' Reading verses 1 to 18 as a doctrine of God, apart from verses 22 to 33, would be a serious mistake.

The counsel of verses 27 to 30, to bear the yoke, sit in silence and offer the cheek, is advice for a people under deserved discipline. It does not tell anyone to accept abuse in silence. Jesus quotes the cheek in Matthew 5:39, yet when He was struck He asked the officer why, John 18:22-23. The prayer for retribution in verses 64 to 66 is recorded as the sufferer's cry, and Romans 12:19 gives the instruction that applies to the believer: leave vengeance to God. What is prescribed is the movement of the whole chapter, from honest complaint to recall of God's character, to waiting, repentance and prayer.

debates.question: Who is the 'man' who has seen affliction?

views.label: Jeremiah, or an individual sufferer
views.case: The specific afflictions of stocks, cistern and mockery fit Jeremiah's life, Jeremiah 20:7 and 38:6, and ancient tradition ascribes the book to him. A single speaker gives the chapter its power.

views.label: A representative figure for the community
views.case: The 'I' turns into 'we' in verses 22 and 40 to 47, and into 'my people' in verses 14 and 48. The man is Israel in the form of one body, a voice for the whole people.

views.label: A royal or Davidic sufferer
views.case: The word for man, geber, the 'rod' of verse 1, and the pattern of a chosen servant under God's anger recall the lament of the anointed king in Psalm 89:38-45. Some have proposed that the speaker is a king, or the king as representative of the people.

debates.bearing: The text deliberately leaves the speaker open so that a reader can step into the place of the sufferer. The three views are not exclusive, and the New Testament will find in one man a place where all three meet.

debates.question: Are verses 55 to 58 a testimony of a past rescue or a confident expectation?

views.label: Past deliverance recalled
views.case: The verbs are in the past: 'You heard my plea,' 'You drew near,' 'You said, Do not be afraid.' The poet speaks as one who has already been brought up out of the pit, perhaps like Jeremiah in Jeremiah 38.

views.label: A confident expression of faith
views.case: The Hebrew perfect verbs can express a settled certainty about what God will do. The prayer of verse 59, 'vindicate my cause!', and the future 'You will pay them back' in verse 64 show that the rescue is still ahead, so the verbs are the language of faith.

debates.bearing: Both readings give the same shape: the poet stands where hearing and deliverance are already real in God's promise, and from there he prays for what remains. The words 'Do not be afraid' are not an answer to a request but an oracle given when the prayer was made, as in Isaiah 41:10.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with a word for 'man' that is not the common one. The sufferer calls himself a geber, a strong man, a man at his full strength, and the word returns in verses 27, 35 and 39 as 'a man' who bears the yoke, who is denied justice and who has no right to complain. Jeremiah 17:5 and 17:7 use it for the man who trusts in man and the man who trusts in the LORD. The poem thus turns a word of strength into a picture of a strong man made low, and the Hebrew sound plays on it, since 'I' is ani and 'affliction' is oni in the first line.

The 'rod' of verse 1 is shevet, the instrument of a ruler or a father. The LORD says of David's son, 'I will discipline him with the rod of men,' 2 Samuel 7:14, and Isaiah 10:5 calls Assyria 'the rod of My anger.' The word links the sufferer to the house of David and to the corrective hand of God.

Three words carry the theology of hope. The first is the verb of verses 21, 24 and 26, yachal, to wait or hope, which is the verb of Psalm 130:5, 'in His word I put my hope.' The second is qavah in verse 25, which pictures a stretched cord and is the verb of Isaiah 40:31, 'those who wait upon the LORD.' Hope in these words is a tension held toward God, not an optimistic mood.

The phrase in verse 21, 'I call this to mind,' is literally 'I bring this back to my heart.' The same idiom appears in Deuteronomy 30:1, where the exiles 'call them to mind in all the nations,' and the promise follows that the LORD will gather them. The sufferer does what Moses said the exiles would do, and in doing so he enters the promise.

Verse 33 says the LORD does not afflict 'willingly.' The Hebrew is literally 'from the heart,' millibbo, and the verb is the root of oni, affliction. God does afflict, but affliction does not arise out of His heart's desire.

In verse 42 the poet says, 'You have not forgiven.' The verb is salach, a word the Old Testament uses of God alone as the one who pardons, as in Numbers 14:19 and Daniel 9:19. The confession puts the people's need exactly where it is: only God can pardon, and He has not yet. The call to 'turn back' in verse 40 is the verb shuv, Jeremiah's own word of repentance, answered by 'Restore us... so we may return' in Lamentations 5:21 and Jeremiah 31:18.

The pit of verses 53 and 55 is bor, a cistern, the same word as the cistern into which Jeremiah was dropped, Jeremiah 38:6, and the 'lowest Pit' of Psalm 88:6.

typology.type: The man under the rod, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: A chosen man suffers under 'the rod of God's wrath,' the very instrument with which 2 Samuel 7:14 says the LORD will discipline David's son. Psalm 89:38-45 laments that God has 'spurned and rejected' His anointed. Isaiah 53:4 says that the Servant was thought 'stricken by God, struck down and afflicted' and that He carried our sorrows. The correspondence is that a representative man bears affliction for the people. The escalation in Christ is that the rod falls on Him for sins that are not His, and the type falls short because the sufferer of Lamentations 3 suffers for his own nation's guilt, verse 39.

typology.type: The cheek given to the striker and the mocking song, verses 14 and 30
typology.fulfillment: The sufferer is a laughingstock who is mocked in song, and he is told to offer his cheek to the one who strikes. In the Passion, Jesus is mocked by passers-by, Matthew 27:39-44, and Psalm 69:12 pictures a man who is 'the song of drunkards.' Isaiah 50:6 describes a servant who offers His back and cheeks, and 1 Peter 2:23 says that Christ 'did not retaliate.' The lesson of the poem becomes the person of Christ, though the difference is that He endures undeserved suffering and so makes the offering of the cheek a redemptive act.

typology.type: The pit, the stone and the waters, verses 53 to 55
typology.fulfillment: The speaker is dropped alive into a pit, stones are cast upon him, waters flow over his head, and he calls out from the lowest depths. Jonah 2:5-6 uses the same imagery for his three days, and Jesus uses Jonah as His sign, saying that the Son of Man will be 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth,' Matthew 12:40. A stone was rolled across His tomb and sealed, Matthew 27:60-66. When He rose, He said to the women, 'Do not be afraid,' Matthew 28:10, the same words the poet hears in verse 57. The type falls short because the pit of the poem threatened a man's life, while Christ went into death itself and came out the other side.

typology.type: Waiting quietly for the salvation of the LORD, verse 26
typology.fulfillment: The poet commends silent waiting for the LORD's salvation. Simeon is the New Testament's picture of it, a man 'waiting for the consolation of Israel,' Luke 2:25, who takes the child in his arms and sees the salvation he has waited for. The Hebrew word for salvation in verse 26 comes from the same root as the name Jesus, so that the one waited for is the one named. The pattern holds, though the poet's waiting was uncertain, as the 'perhaps' of verse 29 shows, while Simeon's was fulfilled in a particular infant.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through its central figure, a man who has seen affliction under God's rod. The word for man, geber, together with the rod and the picture of an anointed one under wrath, puts the sufferer close to the Davidic king of Psalm 89:38-45, who is spurned and rejected by God. Isaiah 53:3-4 is the fullest development: a 'man of sorrows' who carried our sorrows, 'struck down and afflicted' by God. The sufferer of Lamentations 3 is the pattern, and the Servant is the One who fills it.

It leads to Christ through the details of the Passion. The mocking songs of verse 14 are taken up in Psalm 69:12 and in the crowd at the cross, Matthew 27:39-44. The offered cheek of verse 30 is Isaiah 50:6 fulfilled when Jesus was slapped, John 18:22, and 1 Peter 2:23 says that He 'did not retaliate' but 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.' The prayers shut out in verse 8 and heard in verse 56 are the pattern of Hebrews 5:7, where Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.'

It leads to Christ through the pit and the dawn. The sufferer is dropped into a pit, covered with stone, and brought out. Jesus lay in a sealed tomb and rose on the third day, and the first word He says to the frightened is the same as in verse 57, 'Do not be afraid.' Revelation 1:17-18 adds, 'I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.' The God who draws near in verse 57 has come near in the flesh.

It leads to Christ through a tension. Verse 33 says that the LORD 'does not willingly afflict,' and yet Isaiah 53:10 says, 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him.' The two are not contradictory. God's heart is not set on the pain of His creatures, but He wills the Servant's pain because it makes possible the removal of the sin that caused the exile. The cross is the place where God's reluctance to afflict and His determination to save are held together.

A caution is needed. The sufferer of this chapter confesses his own sins and those of the people, verses 39 and 42. Christ suffered for sins not His own, 1 Peter 3:18. The chapter does not predict Him, but it shows the shape of the faith in which He could be recognised, and it gives words for His people to pray when they follow Him through suffering.
study.god:
The chapter holds together the most extreme statements about God that the Bible allows. In verses 1 to 18 He is the one who has driven, walled in, ground down and shot, and the poem does not look for another cause. In verses 37 and 38 the sovereignty is stated as doctrine: 'Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it? Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?' Nothing in this chapter is a mistake or an accident.

Yet in the same chapter God is the one who does not afflict from the heart, verse 33, and who will not cast off forever, verse 31. The poem refuses to resolve the tension by diminishing either side. God's will is behind the suffering, but His heart is toward compassion, and the chapter asks the reader to live in that tension, not to escape it. Verses 34 to 36 add the moral anchor: crushing prisoners, denying justice and subverting a man's lawsuit are things the Lord does not approve. God is not the author of wrong, even though He disciplines through the wrongs of others.

It shows a God who is both far and near. He is 'the Most High,' verses 35 and 38, and He is 'in heaven,' verse 41. He has covered Himself 'with a cloud that no prayer can pass through,' verse 44, and He 'looks down from heaven,' verse 50. Yet in verse 57 He 'drew near.' Prayer is shut out in verse 8 and heard in verse 56, and the poem does not explain how both were true. It lets the experience of grace stand beside the experience of silence.

It shows a God who forgives and who has not yet forgiven, verse 42. The honesty of the poem forbids pretending that mercy is automatic. The ground of hope is not that the people deserve it but that the LORD's character is what Exodus 34:6-7 declared: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger. And it shows a God who is a portion, verse 24, who can be taken as a possession when everything else has been taken away, as the Levites had no inheritance because 'I am your portion,' Numbers 18:20.

For worship, the chapter teaches that a person can praise God from inside suffering without pretending that suffering is good. It teaches us to recall God's character on purpose, to wait for Him without a time limit, and to bring complaint and confession to the same God. The worship it models is a deliberate act of the will, made with tears, and the church has sung it ever since.

crossReferences.note: The LORD describes Himself to Moses as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. Lamentations 3:22-23 is the exile's use of this creed, and the poet finds that what God said of Himself at Sinai is still true after Jerusalem has fallen.

Moses says that when the people call the blessings and curses to mind in the nations where they are banished, the LORD will restore their fortunes and gather them. The sufferer who says 'Yet I call this to mind' in Lamentations 3:21 does what Moses said the exiles would do.

Jeremiah is lowered into a cistern with only mud and sinks in it. The pit of Lamentations 3:53-55 is similar, and Jeremiah's rescue by ropes in Jeremiah 38:10-13 gives one specific shape to the poem's claim, 'You drew near when I called on You.'

Jeremiah says that he is a laughingstock all day long and that the word of the LORD has become a reproach to him. These are the same words as Lamentations 3:14, and the prophet's complaint shows how closely the sufferer's experience matches the weeping prophet's own.

The psalmist waits for the LORD more than watchmen wait for the morning and puts his hope in His word, because with the LORD is loving devotion and abundant redemption. It is a close companion to Lamentations 3:21-26, with the same verb for hope and the same trust in loving devotion.

Micah looks to the LORD and waits for the God of his salvation, admits that he has sinned and must endure the rage of the LORD, and trusts that the LORD will bring him into the light. It joins confession and hope in the same breath, as Lamentations 3:39 to 42 does.

The servant offers his back to those who struck Him and His cheeks to those who tore out His beard. This is the same posture as Lamentations 3:30, though in Isaiah it is the posture of a righteous servant who does not hide His face from scorn and spittle, and the New Testament sees it in Christ.

It was the LORD's will to crush the Servant, and His soul is made a guilt offering. It sits against Lamentations 3:33, where the LORD does not afflict willingly, and shows how the cross can be both the pain God does not delight in and the work He sets Himself to do.

Believers are told not to take lightly the discipline of the Lord, because He disciplines the one He loves and chastises every son He receives. The passage supplies the New Testament frame for Lamentations 3:27 to 33, where bearing the yoke is the road of a son and not a slave.

Paul says that neither death nor life, nor anything in all creation, will separate believers from the love of God in Christ. It is the New Testament answer to Lamentations 3:22, 'we are not consumed,' and gives it a ground that no pit or flood can reach.

The book's final chapter repeats the call of 3:40 as a prayer: 'Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return.' Chapter 3 says 'let us turn back'; chapter 5 asks God to do the turning, which shows that even repentance is received as a gift.

The risen Christ lays His right hand on John and says, 'Do not be afraid.' It is the same word as in Lamentations 3:57, and it comes from the One who has been dead and holds the keys of Death and Hades, the One who has gone to the bottom of the pit and come out.

study.oneStory:
At the centre of the book that records the Old Testament's most complete collapse stands its most quoted line of hope. The structure matters for the whole Bible. The covenant had set a pattern of blessing and curse, with a promise of restoration for those who repent, Deuteronomy 30:1-3. The exile was the curse at its fullest, and the prophets said that return would come only through the compassion of the LORD. Lamentations 3 is the place where a member of the exiled people, in the pit, takes hold of that promise and chooses to wait.

The chapter looks back to Sinai and the golden calf. After Israel's first great rebellion, Moses received the revelation of God as compassionate and gracious, Exodus 34:6-7, and Israel's whole later survival rested on it. Nehemiah, writing after the exile, draws on it again, Nehemiah 9:31. The poet shows that the foundation held through the greatest destruction the covenant ever knew. The new mercies of each morning are the same mercies that carried the people through the wilderness.

It also looks forward. The sufferer of this chapter is a man who bears affliction under a rod, who is mocked, who is cast into a pit and who is heard. The Gospels present Jesus as the one in whom this pattern is complete. He takes the pit, the mockery and the cheek, and He rises. Isaiah 53 connects that suffering to the sin of others. In Christ, the steadfast love that never ceases is not just an attribute but an act, a death and a resurrection.

The end of the story answers the chapter's last cry. The prayer 'Look, O LORD' is replaced by the sight of the face. Revelation 22:4 says that God's servants 'will see His face,' and 21:4 promises that death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more. The man who sat alone in silence, Lamentations 3:28, is gathered into a city where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The mercies that were new every morning in the exile are the first light of a day that never ends, Revelation 22:5.

sermon.title: God's Faithfulness
sermon.why: Listed on Truth For Life's own collection of Alistair Begg's Lamentations sermons as a message on Lamentations 3, this exposition centers on the steadfast love and faithfulness of God at the heart of the chapter, handled in a faithful, gospel centered way.

quiz.q: What makes Lamentations 3 the turning point of the whole book?

options.text: From the deepest personal darkness it rises to the central confession that the LORD's love never ceases and His mercies are new every morning.
options.note: The book's structural and theological center is the hope of 3:22 to 23.

options.text: It moves from despair to hope in the middle of the chapter.
options.note: True, and specifically the hope is grounded in God's steadfast love and faithfulness.

options.text: It finally announces that Jerusalem was never really destroyed.
options.note: The suffering is real; the turn is toward hope in God, not a denial of the ruin.

options.text: It records God promising never to discipline His people again.
options.note: It says He will not cast off forever, not that He will never discipline.

quiz.q: How does the sufferer arrive at hope in verses 21 to 24?

options.text: He deliberately calls God's steadfast love, mercy, and faithfulness to mind, choosing to hope on that ground.
options.note: Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: hope is an act of remembering God's character.

options.text: He decides to focus on God rather than on his pain.
options.note: True, and specifically he anchors to God's covenant love, endless mercy, and faithfulness.

options.text: His circumstances suddenly improved and lifted his mood.
options.note: Nothing in his circumstances changes; the hope comes from remembering who God is.

options.text: He concludes that his suffering was meaningless.
options.note: He finds meaning and hope in God's character, not meaninglessness.

quiz.q: What does it mean to say the LORD is my portion, in verse 24?

options.text: That God Himself, not possessions or circumstances, is one's true and sufficient inheritance and treasure.
options.note: Cheleq is inheritance language; as the Levites' portion was the LORD, so is the sufferer's.

options.text: That God is the most important thing the sufferer has.
options.note: Close, and the specific image is that God is his allotted inheritance, his very portion.

options.text: That God will give him back all his lost property.
options.note: The point is God Himself as the portion, not the return of possessions.

options.text: That he owns a share of God's power.
options.note: It means God is his inheritance, not that he possesses a portion of God's power.

quiz.q: How does the chapter counsel the sufferer to respond to God's discipline?

options.text: To wait quietly for the LORD's salvation, examine and turn from sin, and call on His name from the depths.
options.note: Waiting, repentance, and prayer are the prescribed responses, 3:25 to 26, 3:40, 3:55.

options.text: To be patient and keep trusting God through the suffering.
options.note: True, and more specifically to wait, repent, and cry out to God.

options.text: To demand that God immediately explain everything.
options.note: It counsels quiet waiting and repentance rather than demands.

options.text: To abandon prayer since God had shut it out.
options.note: Though 3:8 felt prayer was shut out, the sufferer keeps calling and God draws near, 3:55 to 57.

quiz.q: How does the sufferer's cry from the pit point to Christ?

options.text: The innocent one cast into the pit, with waters over his head, who calls out and is heard, foreshadows Christ, who went into death and was raised by the Father.
options.note: Christ is the true sufferer heard from the depths, met with Do not be afraid.

options.text: It shows a suffering man rescued by God after crying out.
options.note: True, and the pattern is fulfilled supremely in the death and resurrection of Christ.

options.text: It teaches that God never lets the righteous suffer at all.
options.note: The righteous do suffer here; the hope is that God hears and delivers, ultimately in Christ.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: The church has long heard the voice of the suffering Christ in this chapter.

quiz.q: How do the tender mercies of God and the prayer against the enemies fit together?

options.text: The sufferer does not take revenge but entrusts justice to the righteous Judge, which flows from, rather than contradicts, trusting God's mercy.
options.note: He hands the enemies' malice to God, the pattern Christ Himself followed.

options.text: He leaves the enemies to God rather than repaying them himself.
options.note: True, and this entrusting of justice to God is itself part of resting in His faithfulness.

options.text: They simply contradict each other and cannot both be true.
options.note: Scripture holds them together: longing for mercy and for justice against real evil.

options.text: It shows the sufferer taking personal vengeance.
options.note: He asks God to judge; he does not avenge himself.

questions: The sufferer describes his pain with brutal honesty before he ever speaks of hope. Why might it matter that the Bible lets us say how bad it really is before pointing us to God's mercy?
Verse 21 says, yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope. What truths about God's character do you most need to deliberately call to mind when your feelings are telling you all is lost?
His mercies are new every morning. How would it change your ordinary mornings to receive each new day as a fresh delivery of God's compassion rather than just another round of demands?
To say the LORD is my portion is to treasure God more than what He gives. Honestly, is God your portion, or are you leaning your hope on something He might take away?
The sufferer entrusted the wrong done to him to God the Judge rather than avenging himself. Where do you need to hand a grievance over to God instead of carrying or repaying it yourself?

translationNotes.note: Loving devotion translates chesed, God's steadfast covenant love; the range of meaning includes love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and loyalty to a covenant.
Great is Your faithfulness, emunah, gave the title to the beloved hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness; the word denotes firm, dependable reliability.
He does not willingly afflict is literally He does not afflict from His heart; God's discipline is real but not something He delights to do.
